newsitem.title: PERU: American nations to juggle old woes, new vogues.
newsitem.headline: American nations to juggle old woes, new vogues.

text.p: Pledging action, not words and set to juggle a large range of issues from drugs to debt, delegates from the 34 Organisation of American States (OAS) nations arrived during the weekend for their 27th annual assembly.
"Things won't stay on paper in the new OAS," promised Beatriz Ramacciotti, ambassador to the OAS for Peru, which is hosting the six-day conference that formally opens on Sunday.
Traditional problems plaguing the region for decades -- principally narco-trafficking, corruption, rights abuses and poverty -- were set to dominate the assembly's 75-point agenda.
But the new moves toward regional trade accords and free-market reforms were also expected to figure high.
"It's a large agenda preceded by many months of work," OAS Secretary General Cesar Gaviria told local radio station Radio Programas del Peru after his arrival in Lima.

"There is such a multitude of meetings these days that the OAS must see how it can become the epicentre of debate and solutions. If it does that, it is going to be a great political and economic institution," he added.

Another pressing issue is the $98 million in membership quotas owed by OAS nations. The leading debtor is the United States with $55.6 million, followed by Brazil at $15.9 million and Canada at $6.8 million.
Often lambasted as a talking-shop with little real influence, the century-old OAS is determined to use the Lima assembly to change its image.

"The OAS has overcome the burdened structure of the past through a concerted effort ... despite the asymmetries that persist between its member countries," said Ramacciotti in a meeting with journalists.
One of those "asymmetries" is the delicate and often thorny relationship between the United States and its Latin American and Caribbean neighbours.
While most countries sent their foreign ministers to the assembly, Washington dispatched White House special adviser for Latin American affairs Thomas "Mack" McLarty.

He was due to travel to the border between Peru and Ecuador during the week to inspect peace-keeping efforts on their disputed frontier. The two countries went to war in 1995 over a long-running border conflict that has exemplified just the sort of antagonism the OAS wants to eliminate.
The Peruvian government, still reeling from the four-month Lima hostage crisis, staged a huge security operation to prevent leftist guerrillas from sabotaging the assembly.
Both the Maoist Shining Path and the smaller Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) were planning attacks in Lima around this time, according to anti-terrorist police sources.

It was the MRTA that stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in December, holding 72 VIP hostages for 126 days before troops stormed the building, killed the rebels and freed all but one of the captives.
Arriving OAS delegates were given a security advice list advising them where not to go in Lima, and how to avoid having their hotel room broken into while out and how to fend off unwelcome visitors.
"But the most worrying of the recommendations is to update beforehand all their important documents, including wills," wrote Peruvian magazine Caretas, which published the list.

One hostage crisis hero, Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, was due to chair the OAS assembly. One of the most high-ranking of the MRTA's hostages, Tudela narrowly escaped the residence alive after he was shot twice and a grenade exploded at his side in the rescue operation.
Tudela returned to the foreign ministry last week and still uses a wheelchair.
